explanations.answer: Ahab's silver and gold and his family
explanations.explanation: Ben-hadad's message says, “Your silver and gold are mine, and your best wives and children are mine!” (1 Kings 20:3). Silver, gold and family, all claimed in one breath. That's a lot of claiming from a man standing outside the wall. And he says it like he's reading off a receipt.

explanations.answer: Ahab's horses and chariots and his land
explanations.explanation: Horses and chariots are already on Ben-hadad's side, since the thirty-two kings brought theirs (1 Kings 20:1). What he claims from Ahab is “Your silver and gold” and “your best wives and children” (1 Kings 20:3). Land never comes up in his message. Keep your eyes on that list, friend, because the list is the whole message.

explanations.answer: Ahab's fields and flocks and his cities
explanations.explanation: No fields, flocks or cities in this message. Ben-hadad says, “Your silver and gold are mine, and your best wives and children are mine!” (1 Kings 20:3). That's a short list, but I think it's a list that hits close to home. Short doesn't mean small, friend.

explanations.answer: He agrees to all of it
explanations.explanation: Ahab answers, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” (1 Kings 20:4). No haggling and no counteroffer. He even calls Ben-hadad “my lord the king.” Later Ahab reminds the elders, “…I did not deny him.” (1 Kings 20:7), so that yes was a real yes.

explanations.answer: He refuses every bit of it
explanations.explanation: Not at this point. In 1 Kings 20:4 Ahab says, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” The no shows up later, and Ahab says it about “this thing,” not the whole list (1 Kings 20:9). Right now it's a yes, friend, and that's the surprise.

explanations.answer: He asks for a few days to think
explanations.explanation: Ahab doesn't ask for time. His reply is, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” (1 Kings 20:4). The only clock in sight is Ben-hadad's “about this time tomorrow” in 1 Kings 20:6. I think I'd have asked for time with that army outside my window, but that's me.

Ben-hadad's message says, “But about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to search your palace and the houses of your servants.” (1 Kings 20:6). Tomorrow, friend, not next week. A whole week would be a calm kind of threat. This one fits on a sticky note for tomorrow morning.

Ben-hadad says, “But about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to search your palace and the houses of your servants.” (1 Kings 20:6). That's one day, not a week. Even the cable guy gives you a longer window than that, and he's never on time.

Ahab summons “all the elders of the land” (1 Kings 20:7). He tells them, “Please take note and see that this man is looking for trouble…” It's the group chat of its day, friend: “Y'all seeing this?” The elders and the people give their answer in the next verse (1 Kings 20:8).

Ahab doesn't summon prophets here. He summons “all the elders of the land” (1 Kings 20:7). A prophet does show up later, but he's the one who approaches Ahab (1 Kings 20:13). Different verse, different visitor, friend.

Priests don't appear in this scene. Ahab summons “all the elders of the land” (1 Kings 20:7). Priests turn up in the Bible a lot, so I get the guess, friend. But the verse says elders, and I'm sticking with the verse.

The elders and the people all say, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” (1 Kings 20:8). All of them, friend, and in one voice. Getting a room to agree on the thermostat is harder than that, and this room had a king and an army to face. Ahab had said yes the first time, and now the whole crowd says to stop.

Giving in is what Ahab had already done when he said, “I am yours, along with all that I have.” (1 Kings 20:4). The elders and the people say the opposite: “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” (1 Kings 20:8). That's a full turn from where Ahab started, friend.

explanations.answer: Pay him to leave the city
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions paying Ben-hadad to leave. The elders and the people say, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” (1 Kings 20:8). Their words are about his terms, and they say not to consent. I know a cheaper deal sounds tempting, friend, but it isn't in the text.

Ahab keeps the first yes. His message is, “All that you demanded of your servant the first time I will do, but this thing I cannot do.” (1 Kings 20:9). The first demand stays a yes, and “this thing” is where he stops. So he doesn't take back everything, friend. It's one line in the sand, not a whole new beach.

Ahab's message says, “All that you demanded of your servant the first time I will do, but this thing I cannot do.” (1 Kings 20:9). The first yes stands. He draws the line only at “this thing.” That's a careful sentence, friend: two halves, one yes and one no.

In his oath, Ben-hadad says, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” (1 Kings 20:10). So the picture is dust, one handful per man. That's a threat measured in handfuls, friend. He's handing out souvenirs, and the souvenir is the city.

Ben-hadad's oath isn't about making Samaria his royal city. It says, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” (1 Kings 20:10). A royal city has walls and rooms. Dust has neither, friend.

explanations.answer: It'll be spared if Ahab bows
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the oath offers to spare Samaria. Ben-hadad says, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” (1 Kings 20:10). There's no “bow and I'll back off” in there. It's all dust, friend.

Ahab's message reaches Ben-hadad “while he and the kings were drinking in their tents” (1 Kings 20:12). That's thirty-two kings plus Ben-hadad, friend. I bet the news from Samaria was not the loudest thing in that camp. The detail comes back in 1 Kings 20:16, so hold on to it.

The verse says drinking, not resting. Ben-hadad gets Ahab's message “while he and the kings were drinking in their tents” (1 Kings 20:12). Resting would sound calmer, friend. That drinking detail comes back in 1 Kings 20:16.

Nothing in the verse has these men praying. It says Ben-hadad received the message “while he and the kings were drinking in their tents” (1 Kings 20:12). Praying would've been a whole different tent, friend. This is the drinking tent.

Ben-hadad hears Ahab's message and tells his servants, “Take your positions.” (1 Kings 20:12). Then they station themselves against the city. After that big oath about dust, his actual order is three words. Big oath, small order, friend.

Actually, this one is true. Ben-hadad tells his servants, “Take your positions.” (1 Kings 20:12), and they station themselves against the city. In this verse he doesn't send another message. He just gives the order, friend, and it's a short one.

explanations.answer: Deliver it into Ahab's hand this very day
explanations.explanation: Through the prophet, the LORD says, “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” (1 Kings 20:13). Notice the timing: this very day. Not someday, and not next season. Ahab is looking at a huge army, and the promise is for today.

explanations.answer: Send it back home to Aram
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say anything about sending the army home. He says, “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” (1 Kings 20:13). “Into your hand” means into Ahab's hand. That's a lot closer than Aram, friend.

explanations.answer: Let it take the city for a while
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say the army gets a turn with the city. He says, “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” (1 Kings 20:13). Delivering an army into Ahab's hand is not letting it keep Samaria, friend. “This very day” is the part I'd underline.

explanations.answer: The young officers of the district governors
explanations.explanation: Ahab asks, “By whom?” and the prophet answers, “This is what the LORD says: ‘By the young officers of the district governors.’” (1 Kings 20:14). That's the LORD's pick. Me, I'd have gone looking for the biggest sword in the room, which is why nobody hands me the battle plans.

explanations.answer: The elders and the people of the land
explanations.explanation: The elders and the people spoke up earlier, when they told Ahab not to consent to Ben-hadad's terms (1 Kings 20:8). But when Ahab asks, “By whom?” the prophet names “the young officers of the district governors” (1 Kings 20:14). Different job, different people, friend. The elders gave their advice, and someone else gets the assignment.

explanations.answer: A band of prophets of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Only one prophet shows up in this scene, and he's the one speaking to Ahab (1 Kings 20:13). When Ahab asks, “By whom?” the answer is “the young officers of the district governors” (1 Kings 20:14). No band of prophets here. A whole band would've been quite the entrance, friend.

Ahab asks, “Who will start the battle?” and the prophet answers, “You will.” (1 Kings 20:14). The man who asks who goes first is the man who goes first. Friend, I know that feeling. Ask who's carrying the heavy box and suddenly it's you.

The elders spoke earlier, when they said not to consent to Ben-hadad's terms (1 Kings 20:8), but they aren't named for starting the battle. When Ahab asks who will start it, the prophet says, “You will.” (1 Kings 20:14). Giving advice is one job and going first is another, friend. Ahab gets the answer to his own question.

Ben-hadad is the one with the army around Samaria (1 Kings 20:1), but that isn't what the prophet answers. Ahab asks, “Who will start the battle?” and the prophet says, “You will.” (1 Kings 20:14). The surrounded king gets the first move, friend. That's a twist.

The 232 go first, but they aren't alone. After them, Ahab assembled “the rest of the Israelite troops, 7,000 in all.” (1 Kings 20:15). When the young officers march out, the army is behind them (1 Kings 20:19). First in line isn't the same as all by yourself, friend.

Ahab assembled the 232 young officers, and after them “the rest of the Israelite troops, 7,000 in all.” (1 Kings 20:15). The 232 lead, and the troops follow, with the army behind them as they march out (1 Kings 20:19). Leading is lonely enough without being alone, friend.

The verse says, “They marched out at noon while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk.” (1 Kings 20:16). Noon, friend. The sun is high and the tents are already busy. I bet that wasn't on anybody's schedule.

Your pick says false, but the verse says it plainly: “They marched out at noon while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk.” (1 Kings 20:16). So it's true. Israel is marching out while Ben-hadad and the kings are in their tents. I bet they didn't see this noon coming, friend.

Ben-hadad hears about the men marching out and says, “If they have marched out in peace, take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” (1 Kings 20:18). Peace or war, he gives the same order. That's one answer for two very different situations, friend.

explanations.answer: Strike them down at the gate
explanations.explanation: That order isn't in the text. Ben-hadad says, “If they have marched out in peace, take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” (1 Kings 20:18). Alive both times, friend. Whatever else he had in mind, the order he gives is to take them alive.

explanations.answer: Pull back and let them pass
explanations.explanation: Pulling back isn't the order. Ben-hadad says, “If they have marched out in peace, take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” (1 Kings 20:18). That's reaching out, not stepping aside. He wants them caught, friend, whichever kind of marching it is.

The verse says, “…each one struck down his opponent. So the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit.” (1 Kings 20:20). Notice the “So.” First the young officers strike, then the Arameans flee. Nobody sticks around to ask for a manager, friend.

The Arameans don't regroup in this verse. They flee, with the Israelites in pursuit (1 Kings 20:20). Regrouping takes people standing still long enough to talk it over, and nobody's standing still, friend.
Surrender isn't what happens. The verse says, “So the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit.” (1 Kings 20:20). Surrendering means stopping, and these men are running. Big difference, friend.

Ben-hadad isn't captured. The verse says, “But Ben-hadad king of Aram escaped on horseback with the cavalry.” (1 Kings 20:20). This is the same Ben-hadad who was in a tent a few verses ago, now riding off on a horse. Quite a change of seating, friend.

Same verse: “But Ben-hadad king of Aram escaped on horseback with the cavalry.” (1 Kings 20:20). The Arameans flee, but their king rides away. From the tent to the saddle in one story, friend. That's a busy day for him.
